title: Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum value in each contiguous window of size k as the window slides from left to right.

s1_definition.profdef: Sliding Window Maximum uses a monotonic decreasing deque of indices to report the maximum of each window of size k in linear time. The deque front always holds the index of the current window's maximum, you remove indices that fall out of the window from the front, and you remove smaller trailing indices from the back before adding each new element.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya watches a live feed of per-second trade prices and wants, for every sliding window of the last k seconds, the highest price in that window. She keeps a short list of "candidate highs" ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new price arrives, any smaller candidates at the back are now useless because the newer price is both larger and more recent, so she discards them. She also drops the front candidate once it ages out of the window. The front of the list is always the window maximum.
s1_definition.oneliner: Maintain a decreasing deque of indices, drop stale indices from the front and smaller indices from the back, and the front is always the window maximum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sliding Window Maximum uses a monotonic decreasing deque of indices to report the maximum of each window of size k in linear time. The deque front always holds the index of the current window's maximum, you remove indices that fall out of the window from the front, and you remove smaller trailing indices from the back before adding each new element.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya watches a live feed of per-second trade prices and wants, for every sliding window of the last k seconds, the highest price in that window. She keeps a short list of "candidate highs" ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new price arrives, any smaller candidates at the back are now useless because the newer price is both larger and more recent, so she discards them. She also drops the front candidate once it ages out of the window. The front of the list is always the window maximum.

**One line to remember:** Maintain a decreasing deque of indices, drop stale indices from the front and smaller indices from the back, and the front is always the window maximum.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach scans each window for its maximum, costing k work per window and quadratic overall. A heap improves this but costs n-log-k. The monotonic deque achieves true linear time because each index enters and leaves the deque exactly once.

You store indices, not values, so you can tell when an index has slid out of the window. Before adding the current index, you remove from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the current value, because they can never be the maximum while the current, larger and newer, element is in the window. For example: `while (!deque.isEmpty() && nums[deque.peekLast()] <= nums[i]) deque.pollLast();`.

Then you add the current index to the back. For example: `deque.offerLast(i);`.

You remove from the front any index that has fallen outside the window, meaning its index is less than or equal to `i - k`. For example: `if (deque.peekFirst() <= i - k) deque.pollFirst();`.

Once the window is fully formed, meaning `i >= k - 1`, the front of the deque is the index of the maximum, so you record `nums[deque.peekFirst()]`. For example: `result[i - k + 1] = nums[deque.peekFirst()];`.

The time complexity is linear because every index is added once and removed once. The space is bounded by the window size. A senior nuance is why the deque stays decreasing: removing smaller trailing elements guarantees the front is always the largest in the current window, and because newer elements that are larger make older smaller elements permanently irrelevant, discarding them never loses a future maximum.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India's trading desk, Priya monitors a live per-second price feed and needs a rolling peak price over the last k seconds to drive a trailing-stop alert. Recomputing the max of every window from scratch cannot keep up with a high-frequency feed. This is exactly how Sliding Window Maximum works — a monotonic deque yields each window's peak in constant amortized time.

Problem 2 — Old prices must stop counting the instant they age out of the window, and newer higher prices must immediately dominate older lower ones. This is exactly the deque discipline of dropping stale indices from the front and smaller indices from the back.

The mini-project builds a `RollingPeakFinder` that computes each window maximum with a monotonic deque, a `TrailingStopService` that reports rolling peaks for alerting with logging, and a runnable demo over a short price feed.

sections.s5_journey:
The input feed is 1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7 with window size 3.

Step 1: Index 0, value 1. The deque is empty, add index 0. The deque holds 0. Window not yet complete.

Step 2: Index 1, value 3. 3 is greater than or equal to value 1 at index 0, so remove index 0 from the back. Add index 1. The deque holds 1. Still not complete.

Step 3: Index 2, value -1. -1 is not greater than value 3 at index 1, so add index 2. The deque holds 1, 2. The window is now complete; the front is index 1 with value 3, so the first window maximum is 3.

Step 4: Index 3, value -3. Add index 3. The deque holds 1, 2, 3. The front index 1 is not yet out of the window because 1 is greater than 3 minus 3 which is 0. The window maximum is 3.

Step 5: Index 4, value 5. 5 is greater than or equal to the back values -3, then -1, then 3, so remove indices 3, 2, and 1 from the back. Add index 4. The deque holds 4. The window maximum is 5.

Step 6: Index 5, value 3. 3 is not greater than value 5 at index 4, so add index 5. The deque holds 4, 5. The window maximum is 5.

Step 7: Index 6, value 6. 6 is greater than or equal to value 3 at index 5 and value 5 at index 4, so remove both. Add index 6. The deque holds 6. The window maximum is 6.

Step 8: Index 7, value 7. 7 removes index 6 from the back. Add index 7. The deque holds 7. The window maximum is 7. The result is 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7.

```text
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Rolling Peak for Trailing Stop
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z [INFO] Feed [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7] rolling peaks (k=3) = [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
```

```text
    ├─ i6 v6  pop5,4 add     dq:[6]  → max=6
    ├─ i7 v7  pop6 add       dq:[7]  → max=7
    ▼
  result: [3,3,5,5,6,7]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Sliding Window Maximum ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Monotonic DECREASING deque of indices                    │
  │  Front = current window max; back = newest candidates     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Finder computes peaks; Service drives alerting        │
  │  O: window size is a parameter, not hardcoded             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   RollingPeakFinder                   │
  │  + maxOfEachWindow(prices, k): int[]  │ O(n) time, O(k) space
  │    - deque: Deque<Integer> (indices)  │ values decreasing
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Three deque rules per element i:
    1. pollLast while prices[last] <= prices[i]  (keep decreasing)
    2. offerLast(i)
    3. pollFirst if peekFirst() <= i - k         (drop stale)
    then record prices[peekFirst()] once i >= k-1

  Contract: result[j] = max of window starting at index j.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Maximum is the problem that showcases the monotonic deque, which beats both the naive per-window scan and the heap-based approach by achieving true linear time. I keep a double-ended queue of indices maintained so the values they point to are decreasing from front to back, which means the front always holds the index of the maximum in the current window.

There are three disciplined operations per element. Before adding the current index, I remove from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the current value, because a newer and larger element makes those older smaller elements permanently irrelevant. Then I add the current index to the back. Finally I remove the front index if it has aged out of the window, and once the first full window is formed, I record the value at the front as that window's maximum.

Storing indices rather than values is essential, because it is the index that tells me when an element has slid out of the window. The complexity is linear because each index is added once and removed once, and the deque never holds more than one window's worth of candidates, so the extra space is bounded by the window size.

In my project at National Bank of India's trading desk, I used this on a live per-second price feed to maintain a rolling peak price over the last k seconds, which drives a trailing-stop alert. A high-frequency feed makes recomputing each window's maximum from scratch impossible to keep up with, and the monotonic deque gave the current peak in constant amortized time per tick, so the alert fired the instant the price fell a set distance below the rolling peak.
